Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Friday, 18 October 2024 at 11.30am
(Day 058)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu SC with
Ms Emily Aitken for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR MUSTON: This morning we've got in person Dr Michelle
McRae, and on the screen, Dr Natalie Rainger.
<MICHELLE YVONNE McRAE, affirmed: [11.31am]
<NATALIE SHERIDAN RAINGER, affirmed:
MR MUSTON: I might start with you, Dr McRae, could you
state your full name for the record,
DR McRAE: Michelle Yvonne McRae.
MR MUSTON: You are a dermatologist practising from
Pinnacle Dermatology in the New South Wales town of Orange?
DR McRAE: Yes.
MR MUSTON: You are also a clinical lecturer for the
University of Sydney?
DR McRAE: Yes.
MR MUSTON: And you are currently the senior director of
training for the Australasian College of Dermatologists.
DR McRAE: Yes.
MR MUSTON: You've prepared a statement to assist the
Inquiry with its work dated 17 July 2024
DR McRAE: Correct.
MR MUSTON: Have you had an opportunity to review that
statement again before giving your evidence today?
DR McRAE: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Are you satisfied that its contents are, to
the best of your knowledge, true and correct?
DR McRAE: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Thank you.
That's behind tab H7.8, Commissioner.

THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Dr Rainger, could you state your full name for
the record, please.
DR RAINGER: Natalie Sheridan Rainger.
MR MUSTON: I'm going to struggle to pronounce this. I
should have practised before. You are a consultant
otolaryngologist?
DR RAINGER: Otolaryngologist, yes.
MR MUSTON: And head and neck surgeon practising in
Orange?
DR RAINGER: Correct.
MR MUSTON: You have prepared a statement to assist the
Inquiry with its work dated 28 July 2024?
DR RAINGER: Yes.
MR MUSTON: Have you had an opportunity to review that
before giving your evidence today?
DR RAINGER: I have.
MR MUSTON: You are satisfied that its contents are, to
the best of your knowledge, true and correct?
DR RAINGER: Actually since that statement, my position
has changed. I'm no longer the supervisor of training.
I've moved to head of department. That's the only thing.
MR MUSTON: So you formerly held the role of training
supervisor within the Australasian Society of
Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery?
DR RAINGER: Yes, correct.
MR MUSTON: You no longer hold that role; you are now in
the head of department role?
DR RAINGER: Yes, and you can't concurrently hold both, so
I've stepped down from my supervisor of training, but

I still am the surgical supervisor for the medical students
at the University of Sydney on the Orange campus still.
MR MUSTON: Thank you.
Commissioner, that statement is behind tab L9.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, I have that one.
MR MUSTON: While we're on your statement, Dr Rainger,
could I ask you to turn to paragraph 14?
DR RAINGER: So the one starting, "In my experience"?
MR MUSTON: "In my experience", yes. You tell us about
some of the challenges that you perceive that would arise
if you weren't visiting satellite hospitals as
a specialist, or a specialist ceased visiting satellite
hospitals, and you point to the risk of GPs becoming
deskilled and leaving communities.
Could I ask you, first of all, to explain what you
mean by satellite hospitals and the work that is being
done, and then why that has the capacity to produce the
result of deskilling and a downturn in the population of
GPs in these communities?
DR RAINGER: Sure. So the Western area health district is
a very large district spread across a long area. We
provide the ENT service from Blue Mountains right through
to Bourke and Broken Hill, which is covered by Adelaide, so
many areas that are still remote to us, as well. As part
of that service, we do both consulting and peripheral
operating at smaller hospitals within the LHD.
For example, I travel to Cowra once a month where I do
an operating list, which is staffed by the GPs in that
town. So they are what we call GP anaesthetists. They
will provide the anaesthesia for the operation as well as
the follow-up and post-op care for these patients. That,
in turn, keeps them upskilled in emergency airway
management and skills like intubating paediatric patients,
which they may have to do in emergency settings on their
own out in those communities.
MR MUSTON: So I gather that if they weren't performing
those procedures out in those satellite hospitals, the

skills that they have as anaesthetists would be lost or
would fade.
DR RAINGER: Yes, unless you're doing something routinely,
if you're not doing a difficult procedure routinely, it's
even harder to do it in an emergency, high-stress-filled
situation, where a child might be dying in front of you.
So being able to do it in a routine, elective setting,
keeps them upskilled. If you don't use those skills, you
lose them. These little communities rely very heavily on
sometimes what is their sole practitioner, and I strongly
believe if communities don't have medical services, then
you have a drift of population moving away from those small
communities.
MR MUSTON: And what is it about the ability to use those
skills and keep them up to date that, in your view, that is
keeping GPs working in some of these communities? Perhaps
to put it another way. Why is it that if they weren't able
to use these skills in the satellite hospitals that they
are located near, GPs would be leaving these communities?
DR RAINGER: A GP's work is extremely onerous and their
role with face-to-face consulting with patients is a huge
amount of what they do, but they also provide a 24/7
on-call service to that area, so they need to be able to
manage the emergency things that come in after hours to
stabilise patients enough to transfer them to a tertiary
centre.
So I can imagine that is quite daunting and, you know,
a hugely arduous task, but by giving themselves skills
across lots of different areas, like obstetrics and ENT and
scopes and procedural skills, it just further bolsters
their confidence in their ability to look after their
community.
MR MUSTON: Dr McRae, I see you are nodding. That accords
with your view and experience of practising in a rural
area?
DR McRAE: Absolutely. Throughout my training from
medical student through to now, having exposure as
a medical student to those small clinics and visiting with
the surgeons and observing those GPs assisting in those
various areas, particularly in theatre as GP anaesthetists
and O&G, provides ongoing community support when they

really need it.
DR RAINGER: I think as well, also, it's not just the GPs,
that then entails a whole theatre workforce being employed
that day, and so it gives back to the community as well,
local jobs for local people.
MR MUSTON: Is there an extent to which the ability for
that whole workforce to participate in procedures and the
like keeps the job interesting and attracts them to keep
doing it in circumstances where, if they were just, say,
doing other work that one might associate with a small
country facility, it would be harder to attract staff to do
the more run of the mill day-to-day work?
DR RAINGER: Absolutely. Look, I can't speak for the GPs
individually, but myself as a surgeon, I know that I really
look forward to my procedural days. The face-to-face
consulting days can be a long grind, so I think people,
when they learn skills, like to keep using them and be
useful. Part of what we do, I guess.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the role that you have, or your
practice as a VMO, you have told us in your statement that
if a position had been available to you as a staff
specialist, you would happily have taken it. Can I ask,
would that, at least in your experience, be a relatively
rare thing, for a surgeon to be a staff specialist within
the public system in New South Wales?
DR RAINGER: There's a mix. There certainly are staff
specialists, especially in the bigger tertiary centres in
Sydney. I can really only attest to Orange and our
workforce out here. Our surgeons are all VMOs, I think,
100 per cent. We have staff specialists among the
physicians, but I think all of our surgeons are VMOs.
MR MUSTON: When you were first commencing your practice
out there, what was it that made being a staff specialist,
if that were able to have been accommodated, attractive
from your perspective?
DR RAINGER: I think back then I probably didn't have
a very good understanding of how the business side of
public health works, so I was probably very naive, and
I was interested in exploring whatever options were
available to us. But I certainly liked the idea of being

able to provide a public service to a rural community.
I think that's so important. I feel like our patients out
here deserve the same level of care as someone, you know,
in a city centre would receive. So I guess that's still an
ongoing journey. You know, as part of that we still don't
have our public clinics up and running, and if we had been
able to take that staff specialist role from the beginning,
that may have been an easier journey.
I don't know if I would necessarily go down that path
now, but I think the funding to develop the public service
would have been easier from a staff specialist's viewpoint
rather than a VMO.
MR MUSTON: Dr McRae, I imagine that a staff specialist
position as a dermatologist within a town like Orange was
not something that you saw as a realistic way of practising
in a town like that?
DR McRAE: It's extraordinarily unlikely, given that there
are only a couple in New South Wales, in Sydney. It's very
unusual for a dermatologist to have a staff specialist
role, because it's a very different approach to other
specialties such as surgery or physicians, which are
considered as necessary in a hospital, and I would argue
that some hospitals don't see dermatology as a specialty
that is necessary, so we're lucky to have a seat at the
table, let alone have a full-time staff specialist
position.
THE COMMISSIONER: Why wouldn't hospitals see having
a dermatologist as necessary?
DR McRAE: I have, for the last 10 years, tried to obtain
a VMO paid position at the hospital. We did have a clinic
running when I first went back as a fourth-year registrar
and I was offered a position that they were going to
advertise for. The advertisement was never put through,
and that money was then - when I asked, "Why wasn't the ad
put up", "They gave the funding to ED", was what we were
told. Dermatology --
THE COMMISSIONER: So it can't be because skin conditions
can't be very serious?
DR McRAE: It's not because skin conditions aren't very
serious, it's because we're not seen as making the hospital

any money. In our clinic, our billings, we were told, did
not make enough money to cover our costs. The problem was
that the person doing the billings, who was an admin
officer, had incorrectly done billings and only had earned
$75 for the clinic, for example, in one clinic, and hadn't
resubmitted the billings to Medicare, in error.
So this is NSW Health policy now to bill to Medicare
for patients seen in the outpatients clinics, and we do
bill the same item numbers for procedures. However,
dermatologists don't do procedures under anaesthetic very
often, so we don't use a theatre and we don't have
anaesthetic item numbers. So our item numbers are limited
from a billing capacity and so, because of that, we were
told we cost too much to have a clinic.
THE COMMISSIONER: Despite the obvious benefits to
population health having dermatology services?
DR McRAE: Despite this. So there was an example of
a patient needing to be transferred to Sydney because they
had a blistering skin condition - and I've been an HMO for
a number of years providing my services on a daily basis on
call. Westmead refused to take the patient because they
said, "You've got a dermatologist in the area", however,
I was not a VMO with the hospital so did not have admitting
rights. That would have saved several thousand in transfer
fees to a Sydney hospital, but they would rather transfer
a sick patient than have someone who was local look after
them.
MR MUSTON: Can I just ask you about your evidence that
there is one dermatologist in each of Albury, Griffith,
Wagga Wagga and Tamworth?
DR McRAE: Full time.
THE COMMISSIONER: Based on the populations of those
regions, how many ideally should there be?
DR McRAE: There should be one per 50,000 people. We
cover an area --
THE COMMISSIONER: How many more should that be? You can
take that on notice, but --
DR McRAE: I cover an area of about - theoretically, my

local health district is 280,000 to 290,000 people. That
is not including the greater Far West area.
THE COMMISSIONER: So there should be five or six of you?
DR McRAE: And I have also patients travelling out of
area, because they cannot access, from the north - Blue
Mountains have no dermatologist and Nepean has only
private. Also from Southern New South Wales I receive from
Hay and Griffith, as well as Canberra and Young and north
to Coonamble, Walgett, Broken Hill, Mudgee and then to
Nepean. So we would cover an area definitely over 350,000
people.
THE COMMISSIONER: Can I also ask you just to explain to
me - in paragraph 9 you've talked about the very long wait
list you have, which is driven by the fact that you can't
divide yourself into two or three or four, and to explain
to me how you manage the triaging and the more urgent
appointments.
Can I give you an example?
DR McRAE: Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: The people here know I like to talk
about my own health conditions, but six or seven years ago
I had something cut out of my forehead, which was I think
a squamous cell carcinoma. Then about six weeks ago I had
a spot on my cheek that my GP thought looked suspicious, so
referred me to a dermatologist, and when I rang, I couldn't
see that dermatologist until December. So I made the
appointment but rang the GP back and said, "Are you worried
about", and he said, "Yes, that's too along, even for a" -
he didn't know what it was. It might have been, he
thought, psoriasis but it looked suspicious. So I was able
to see a different dermatologist very quickly, who took
a biopsy. It turns out to be - they said it was a sunspot.
DR McRAE: Actinic keratosis
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes. He zapped it with liquid
nitrogen, and a few other spots. But say there's someone
with a similar concerning spot like that, is that something
that ought to be seen urgently and how do you manage that
in relation to your referrals, given there's only one of
you for so many people?

DR McRAE: The first thing is it's difficult for GPs to
know everything, and they've got a very broad job to do,
and it's very, very variable --
THE COMMISSIONER: I've had a lot of psoriasis burnt off
with liquid nitrogen, which I don't blame my GP for because
he is excellent otherwise.
DR McRAE: I have a lot of respect - my father-in-law is
a GP in Orange and has been since 1980. I have a lot of
respect for the rural GPs locally. I would say half of
them have my phone number, whether that's a good or a bad
thing, including out to Forbes, Parkes, Cowra and Dubbo.
So I've already been contacted this morning by two GPs.
So I guess, one, we, or I, manage this by triaging
every week, if not daily. We will ask patients or GPs to
send us a photo of the lesion first, and if it's not a good
photo, then they come in and we book them as an urgent in
what I call my "nursing list". We do it as an urgent
consult, so it's not a full review but obviously when
patients come and they're covered in spots on their whole
head, I'm not looking at one spot, I'm looking at a lot of
things.
So I guess I have skates on every day. But we do try
and fit in all urgents as requested. So I'm currently
working five days a week seeing patients.
THE COMMISSIONER: I imagine managing that is difficult.
You are already have an enormous wait list.
DR McRAE: I have extremely good staff and I have
increased capacity, probably a little bit to my own
detriment, in terms of accepting and taking on the
accreditation of training a registrar, and I've also
sponsored an IMG this year as well.
THE COMMISSIONER: But going back, if we can go back to
your original point about dermatologists not making
money --
DR McRAE: For the hospital.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, for the hospital. I'm right,
aren't I, that that's absolutely purely a decision that is

made on the basis of financial matters, not because --
DR McRAE: Not because of demand.
THE COMMISSIONER: -- patients can't present with
conditions of the skin that are life threatening; correct?
DR McRAE: That's correct. So dermatology conditions can
be life threatening; many drug reactions are life
threatening, and that's not within melanoma and all the
skin cancers --
THE COMMISSIONER: And not just life threatening but
needing urgent medical attention?
DR McRAE: Needing urgent attention. I do receive
multiple email consults and phone consults from the
hospital each week, that I'm keeping a tally of, that
I provide advice regarding dermatological management on the
wards.
THE COMMISSIONER: Tell me if I'm wrong, you'll know much
better than me, but Australia as a country has relatively
high rates of skin cancers that are very serious; correct?
DR McRAE: That's correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes.
DR McRAE: And are underestimated.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes. That's enough about me.
MR MUSTON: You've told us about the waiting lists and
I think also about the way in which you approach charging
patients, both at one end of the spectrum bulk billed, and
at the other end charged as a private patient. What's the
decision-making process within your practice around where
someone sits on that spectrum?
DR McRAE: I have a similar arrangement with Natalie,
longstanding, any Aboriginal Medical Service patient is
bulk billed. Given that I'm from the area - I will
clarify, I was born and grew up in Narromine, which is west
of Dubbo, and went to school in Orange and lived in
Blayney, which is the size of Narromine, 3,500 people -
I understand the area and where people live and where they

come from. That's not to make judgment on their
background, but I do understand grossly the socioeconomic
problems within different areas, and half my family still
lives in Narromine and Dubbo.
My staff are long-term staff, in terms of we don't
lose staff, we treat them very well, we pay them well, and
they own the business with us in terms of they also
understand the patients and understand the area. So when
it comes to patients, I did an audit a couple of years ago
and 60 per cent of my follow-up patients were not full
charge or full billed, meaning they were not billed at the
standard follow-up rate, which is quite high.
I did that out of curiosity more than anything, and
that was just to see, I guess, where we might be sitting
compared to other areas. I was actually looking at it from
a research point of view with a junior doctor, however, I'm
not sure if that's something we want to publish to other
doctors, because it may turn them off.
But the way we do determine it is I have a four-tier
billing system that is actually stipulated in terms of
amounts, from full fee, pension, concession and bulk bill,
and if patients ask or the GP asks for them to be looked
after, then we do; if a patient asks on the day, then we
also do; or if they speak to the staff and indicate that
they wouldn't be able to have a biopsy because they can
only afford the consult fee, then we also still look after
them, because they need the biopsy.
MR MUSTON: Given the 12-month waiting list and the
relatively high proportion of your patients who are sitting
in that towards the bulk billing end of the spectrum, would
it be an oversimplification to say that there would be
sufficient demand in your region for a public dermatology
clinic?
DR McRAE: Absolutely. There was a public dermatology
clinic for a number of years, fortnightly, until we lost
that support. I actually set up a public dermatology
clinic, because I felt there was a need, through the
Aboriginal Medical Service a number of years ago, and ran
that for two and a half years, and it was a very enjoyable
clinic. What actually led to me closing it was the
logistics of referrals if I needed to do a procedure in my
rooms. So if I saw the patient on that day in the

Aboriginal Medical Service and then needed to do
a specialised procedure on them, I had to then take them
back to my rooms. To get a referral from the GP for
a different site is involved, and that was actually the
biggest logistical issue.
So I still look after all those patients in my rooms,
however, I would agree that culturally it's not what they
would consider a culturally safe space compared to the
Aboriginal Medical Service, and I'm actually in the
process, through another initiative with the college, of
setting up another Aboriginal Medical Service public clinic
in Orange next year.
MR MUSTON: There's obviously a funding component that's
required to set up a public clinic in dermatology, but
there's also presumably a workforce requirement, in that
you can only spread yourself so thin, and in order to run
a public clinic in addition to your own practice with
a 12-month waiting list, from the sounds of things, would
require at least one more dermatologist, if not more?
DR McRAE: We're in the process of obtaining what we call
supervisory capacity, to improve supervision. I am
currently attending Canberra one day a month running
a specialised paediatric dermatology clinic in Canberra.
However, I have resigned from next year so that I can set
up an Orange/Dubbo/Western New South Wales training
program, and I have filled my spot in Canberra, and
probably too well, I filled it with a few people, and
I need to obtain supervision for our area. So I have some
capacity, because I do try and provide a public service
somewhere, even though my rooms do, in kind, provide
a public service as well. But this is also a training
service. So I am constantly training, on a daily basis, to
try and improve long-term capacity.
MR MUSTON: Long-term capacity in terms of training
dermatologists or training local general practitioners up
to a level where they know the point at which they can deal
with something in-house and the point at which they should
be handing it over to you; is that --
DR McRAE: Training dermatology registrars with the
intention of them coming back to the area, predominantly.
So we have several in the program, as current New South
Wales director of training, that are associated with the

area and would like to return to the area, we hope, in
time. That also involves an international medical graduate
from Argentina, and with this training program that's to
involve Orange and Dubbo, we do have several rural trainees
on the program in New South Wales at the moment, and it is
a Catch-22, it's getting enough trainees, but it's also
positions of supervision for those.
MR MUSTON: I might come back to the training in a moment.
Could I ask you, Dr Rainger, in relation to the public
clinic that you tell us about in your statement. Putting
aside, just for the moment, the benefits of a public clinic
in terms of your being able to provide registrar training
in Orange, was there - presumably there was - sufficient
public demand on the clinic that you are seeking to set up
to justify it in terms of delivering on the medical needs
of the population?
DR RAINGER: Absolutely, and like Michelle, we have an
especially vulnerable group of patients out here that
require ENT support, such as children, Indigenous children
with hearing and ear problems. So similar to Michelle,
I run probably even more - so a significant proportion of
our patients are bulk billed. As Michelle said, anyone -
the GP asks, or anyone that asks on the day, anyone the
staff identify as being vulnerable, all AMS patients, are
bulk billed, anyone you know, which in a small country town
adds up to quite a few, so it leaves very few that you do
bill.
I also personally have never billed for a procedure.
So all my procedures, which are probably 75 per cent of the
patients I see, have a procedure here in the rooms, like
Michelle - a biopsy or an ear cleaning or a scope to look
to see if they have a throat cancer - and I have never,
ever billed for a procedure. That's all bulk billing, so
a huge need.
MR MUSTON: So in terms of your attempts to get the public
clinic up and rolling, how does the public need for that
service feature in the discussions that you have with
people within the LHD?
DR RAINGER: I don't think there's any argument that
there's a public need. I think we are in the same position
as Michelle, in that ENT is a sub-specialty. The

sub-specialties don't tend to make the public hospitals
much money. You know, the cost for doing a tonsil and a
grommet is a couple of hundred dollars on MBS, whereas
a cataract or a joint replacement makes the hospital money.
Plus our patients, there's a high proportion of paediatric
patients, so it's workload intensive in that you might do,
you know, 10 small children in a day, but that requires
taking 10 paediatric beds overnight and then that leaves
nothing for, you know, anyone else who might need paeds in
the hospital.
So a lot of it purely comes back to funding. Rather
than a lack of support, it's the direction of how funding
is siphoned.
MR MUSTON: Can I come to the on-call burden that you tell
us about in your statement. You told us of a period in
2021 when you were doing one-to-one on call, and more
recently, a still significantly higher level of on call
than metropolitan colleagues. It seems obvious, but
perhaps you could tell us what needs to be done in order to
alleviate that burden.
DR RAINGER: I think I mentioned in my statement about
critical mass. So we've been enviable in that we've
recently been able to recruit two junior consultants, who
were our registrars 10 years ago and we got on to the
training program, again, both from rural backgrounds.
We're very lucky in that one of them is a head and neck
cancer surgeon, and so he has now returned out here to help
set up a head and neck cancer service through the west.
But again, it can't go forward without funding. He has no
lists and no funding for extra theatre time, so all of
these are very slow projects. But I think once you get to
critical mass, you're more likely to be able to induce
others to come back and join you. No-one's going to move
to an area where they're going to be one-on-one on call.
I think that's madness.
MR MUSTON: In terms of that on call burden, are
registrars able to ease that - that is to say, if you had
registrars on a training pathway in Orange and its
surrounds, is that a way in which that on-call burden might
be able to be eased?
DR RAINGER: Yes, absolutely. Since we were able to
acquire our accredited registrar two years ago - I've been

out here as a consultant for 12 years, and in that 12 years
it's been me first on call every time. You go in for every
small nosebleed, every airway emergency. We cover dental
as well after hours, all the dental emergencies, the facial
traumas, and having a registrar definitely eases that
burden, because you now have a second set of hands.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the training of registrars now
that you do have the ability to employ them out there, or
they are being employed out there, how much of their
training is actually happening in Orange as opposed to
other parts of the state and, in particular, metropolitan
parts of the state?
DR RAINGER: So the ENT program is traditionally
a five-year training program based across Australasia, so
you will be attached to a state and every six months you
move to a different position. For example, New South Wales
also covers Canberra and used to cover Darwin. So our
position has been ratified as what we call a SET-1
position, so it's suitable for a first year trainee, so
they are able to spend six to 12 months out here.
We have expressed our preference that they stay for
12, because then they are more likely to put roots down and
develop a sense of, you know, home with the community. But
at this stage the college has only ratified a six-month
position, again which is really difficult when you're
a young person, moving around, maybe moving family with
you, you have a mortgage elsewhere, you have to pay for
accommodation and still meet that. It's really arduous,
I think.
MR MUSTON: Dr McRae, you tell us about your college's
practice that, ideally, a supervisor should not continue in
that role with a particular trainee for more than six
months.
DR McRAE: That's actually something that I suggested a
little while ago, because we did have some rural training
or registrars who were being sent to rural sites for
a year, and there was one supervisor and one registrar. In
the event that there are any concerns from either side, it
makes it very difficult to implement change or for them to
actually approach ways in which to rectify any concerns.
Currently, as the director of training and being the

chair of the rural and regional committee for the college,
I understood quite acutely how that was affecting the rural
registrars and their experience in some places, because we
are very busy. So I'm currently supervising, full time,
two registrars, and I'm very busy, but I'm also very
conscious of making sure that they're appropriately
supervised and appropriately given time to do certain tasks
or travel to things, whereas I think in some sites,
supervision standards can vary sometimes, or travel.
We had one registrar travelling between two sites that
was more than an hour each way. They were travelling late
after a clinic on one evening to get to the next day's
